terms.def: The smallest amount of energy that colliding particles need to have so that they can react.
The special part of an enzyme where the substrate attaches and the reaction happens.
A reaction where a small molecule joins onto a C=C double bond, so the double bond becomes a single bond.
An organic compound that has an –OH (hydroxyl) group bonded to a carbon atom.
A hydrocarbon with only single bonds between its carbon atoms.
A hydrocarbon that has at least one C=C double bond.
An organic compound that contains a nitrogen atom bonded to carbon atoms, such as the –NH₂ group.
A small molecule with an amine group and a carboxyl group. Many of them join together to make proteins.
An enzyme that breaks down starch into smaller sugar molecules.
The electrode where oxidation happens. It is positive in an electrolytic cell and negative in a galvanic cell.
A measure of how much of the total mass of the reactants ends up in the wanted product, shown as a percentage.
A chemical equation with the same number of each type of atom on both sides.
A renewable fuel made by reacting plant oils or animal fats with an alcohol, forming esters.
Ethanol made from plant material, such as by fermenting glucose, and used as a renewable fuel.
A renewable fuel gas, mostly methane, made when bacteria break down organic waste without oxygen.
A number that links a temperature rise in a calorimeter to the energy added, found using a known amount of electrical energy.
A device used to measure the energy released or absorbed in a reaction by measuring a temperature change.
An organic compound that contains the carboxyl group, –COOH.
A substance that makes a reaction faster by giving it a lower-energy pathway, and is not used up.
The electrode where reduction happens. It is negative in an electrolytic cell and positive in a galvanic cell.
A polymer of glucose that makes up plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest it.
Describes a molecule that cannot be placed on top of its mirror image, for example one with a carbon bonded to four different groups.
A method of separating the parts of a mixture because they move at different speeds through a stationary phase.
The idea that particles react only if they collide with enough energy and with the correct orientation.
A reaction where a substance burns in oxygen and releases energy.
The amount of a substance dissolved in a given volume of solution, often in mol L⁻¹.
A reaction where two molecules join and a small molecule, usually water, is released.
A bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons.
A reaction in which water is removed from a molecule.
A separation of partial positive and partial negative charge across a bond or molecule.
Weak attractions between all molecules, caused by short-lived shifts in electron positions. They get stronger in larger molecules.
A solid conductor, such as a metal or graphite rod, where electrons enter or leave a cell.
The use of electrical energy to force a non-spontaneous chemical reaction to happen.
A liquid or solution containing ions that can move, so it can conduct electricity.
A cell that uses electrical energy from an outside power supply to cause a non-spontaneous reaction.
Describes a reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings. Its ΔH is positive.
The heat energy change of a reaction at constant pressure. It is negative if energy is released.
A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, making reactions in living things faster.
The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system where the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant.
A number that compares product concentrations with reactant concentrations at equilibrium. It changes only with temperature.
How far a reversible reaction has gone, showing whether the mixture contains more reactants or more products.
An organic compound with the –COO– group, made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
A reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol that forms an ester and water.
Describes a reaction that releases energy to the surroundings. Its ΔH is negative.
The electric charge carried by one mole of electrons, about 96 500 coulombs per mole.
A carboxylic acid with a long hydrocarbon chain. It is a building block of fats and oils.
A process where microbes such as yeast break down sugars without oxygen and make ethanol and carbon dioxide.
A non-renewable fuel, such as coal, oil or natural gas, formed over millions of years from ancient living things.
A cell that changes the chemical energy of a fuel directly into electrical energy while fuel and oxygen are supplied.
A specific group of atoms in a molecule that decides how the compound behaves in reactions.
A cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction produces electrical energy.
A simple sugar, C₆H₁₂O₆, that cells use as a source of energy.
An alcohol with three –OH groups. It is part of the structure of triglycerides.
The bond that joins two sugar units together in a carbohydrate.
Designing chemical products and processes so that they use less energy, make less waste and use fewer hazardous substances.
The industrial process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
An equation that shows only the oxidation or only the reduction part of a redox reaction, with electrons.
The energy released when a substance burns completely in oxygen, usually given per mole or per gram.
A catalyst that is in a different phase from the reactants, such as a solid catalyst for gases.
A catalyst that is in the same phase as the reactants.
A compound made only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
A strong attraction between a hydrogen atom attached to O, N or F and a lone pair on O, N or F in another molecule.
A reaction where a molecule is broken down by reacting with water.
Burning in a limited supply of oxygen, which makes carbon monoxide or soot and releases less energy.
A method that uses the absorption of infrared light to show which bonds and functional groups are in a molecule.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.
The standard systematic name of a compound, set by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry.
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to partly oppose the change.
The reactant that is completely used up first, which limits the amount of product that can form.
A graph from a technique that separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio. It shows the molecular mass and fragments.
A graph showing how the energies of the particles in a sample are spread out.
The liquid or gas that moves through the stationary phase in chromatography and carries the sample.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole.
The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
The ion formed when a molecule loses one electron in mass spectrometry. Its m/z gives the molecular mass.
A method that uses the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field to show how atoms are arranged in a molecule.
Describes a molecule or bond with no significant uneven sharing of electrons, and so no partial charges.
Describes a resource that is used up much faster than it can be replaced.
Describes a reaction that does not happen by itself and needs energy to be supplied.
A substance that takes electrons from another species, so it is reduced.
A reaction in which a species loses electrons.
The bond that joins two amino acids together, formed between a carboxyl group and an amine group.
The actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical mass, then multiplied by 100%.
A physical form of matter, such as solid, liquid or gas, with uniform properties.
Describes a molecule or bond with uneven sharing of electrons, so it has a partly positive end and a partly negative end.
A very large molecule made of many small repeating units joined together.
A galvanic cell that cannot be recharged because its reactions cannot be reversed efficiently.
A substance that is made in a chemical reaction.
A large molecule made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. It is needed for structure and many functions in living things.
How fast reactants are used up or products are formed, per unit of time.
A substance that is used up in a chemical reaction.
A reaction in which electrons are transferred, so one species is oxidised and another is reduced.
A substance that gives electrons to another species, so it is oxidised.
A reaction in which a species gains electrons.
Heating a mixture with a condenser attached so that vapours turn back to liquid and return to the flask.
Describes a resource that can be replaced at about the same rate as it is used.
In chromatography, the time a substance takes to pass through the column.
A link between two half-cells that lets ions move so the solutions stay electrically neutral.
A galvanic cell that can be recharged because its reactions can be reversed by applying electricity.
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C.
A carbohydrate polymer of glucose that plants use to store energy.
The solid or liquid that stays fixed in chromatography while the sample passes over it.
The substance that an enzyme acts on.
The total area of a solid that is exposed and can touch other reactants.
The maximum mass of product that could form from the reactants if the reaction went to completion.
A method that finds the concentration of a solution by reacting it with a known volume of another solution of known concentration.
The volume of solution added from the burette to reach the end point in a titration.
A molecule made from one glycerol and three fatty acids, which is the main part of fats and oils.
The electrical energy per unit charge that pushes electrons through a circuit, measured in volts.
